options: A short statement of the mission of an exploratory session: target, resources and information sought
A detailed step-by-step script
A contract between test vendor and client
A list of all defects found
questions.explanation: A charter guides a session without scripting it; the common format is Explore (target) with (resources) to discover (information). Scripts, contracts and defect lists are different artefacts.

questions.prompt: Which is a typical length for a time-boxed exploratory session in session-based test management?
options: About 60 to 120 minutes
Exactly 5 minutes
A full week
No time limit
questions.explanation: Sessions are usually around 60 to 120 minutes, long enough to go deep but short enough to stay focused. 5 minutes is too short for meaningful exploration, and a week or no limit removes the time-box.

questions.prompt: A charter should be broad enough to cover the entire application in a single session.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A charter that covers everything gives no focus and cannot be completed in a time-box. Good charters are scoped to an area, risk or quality characteristic that fits one session.

options: Explore the coupon field at checkout with expired, stacked and malformed codes to discover how discounts are validated
Explore the website to find bugs
Test everything about payments
Explore checkout with every possible input
questions.explanation: The first names a clear target, specific resources and the information sought. The others are vague or unbounded.

questions.prompt: Which metrics are commonly recorded per session in session-based test management? Select all that apply.
options: Time spent on test design and execution
Time spent investigating and reporting bugs
Time spent on setup
Number of keystrokes
questions.explanation: SBTM often splits session time into test, bug investigation and setup (often called TBS metrics) to show how much time went into actual testing. Keystrokes are not a meaningful measure.

questions.prompt: A session sheet shows 70% of time spent on setup because the test data kept resetting. What should the debrief lead to?
options: Raise the environment or data problem as an impediment and fix it before more sessions, since it is reducing real testing time
Ask the tester to work faster
Ignore the metric because setup is part of testing
Lengthen the next session to 8 hours
questions.explanation: The session metrics revealed a blocker. Fixing it improves every future session. Pressuring the tester or lengthening sessions does not address the cause.

questions.prompt: What is a typical output of a debrief besides defect reports?
options: New or revised charters for areas that need more exploration
A finished regression suite
The release decision
A code review
questions.explanation: Debriefs decide follow-up work, often new charters. They do not produce full regression suites, make the release decision alone, or review code.

questions.prompt: A product owner wants to know how much of the new booking feature has been explored. Which approach gives the best answer?
options: Map charters to risks and feature areas, and report sessions completed, coverage notes and open issues per area
Report the number of sessions run
Report the total hours spent
Say exploratory testing cannot be reported
questions.explanation: Linking charters to risks and areas turns sessions into a coverage picture. Counts of sessions or hours alone say nothing about what was covered, and exploratory work can be reported when it is structured.

questions.prompt: Testers on a team write charters like "Explore login" and sessions keep producing few findings. Which change is most likely to help?
options: Write charters around specific risks and hypotheses, e.g. "Explore login with expired sessions and parallel tabs to discover session handling flaws", and review them in refinement
Make sessions longer
Switch entirely to scripted tests
Assign more testers to the same vague charter
questions.explanation: Vague charters give vague sessions. Risk-focused charters with concrete resources and goals sharpen exploration. Longer sessions, more people or abandoning exploration do not fix the lack of direction.
